newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Asian stocks drop as Thailand spillover hits region.
newsitem.headline: Asian stocks drop as Thailand spillover hits region.

text.p: Fears that Thailand's economic slowdown is a harbinger of a regionwide decline sent Asian stock markets broadly lower on Thursday as foreign investors ran for the exits, fund managers and analysts said.

A property crisis in Thailand -- which is facing its slowest economic growth in 10 years -- has led to a scrutiny of potential weaknesses in financial markets in the Philippines, Malaysia and Singapore.
Financial authorities in all four countries have taken measures to quell speculation in their booming property sectors.

"It wouldn't surprise me that some fund managers have thought that enough is enough, and are getting out of the region," said Robert Coombe, executive director of Commerce Asset Fund Managers in Malaysia.
Coombe's Malaysia fund has about $100 million, while his parent company manages tens of billions of dollars in regional funds.
"We certainly haven't been dumping in Asia," Coombe added. "One thing we've been trying to gauge is when Thailand is going to bottom."
At 0531 GMT, the Thai SET index was down 23.99 points or 4.2 percent to 547.31. The already-weakened stock market in Thailand was deluged with more selling this week as the baht came under attack.

The baht bounced back on Thursday following assurances by Prime Minister Chavalit that Thailand has no plans to devalue its baht currency and that he would keep his Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, a government minister said.
The baht was trading around 25.650/25.750 to the dollar in early afternoon compared with 26.330/26.430 late on Wednesday.

Stock market declines were almost across-the-board in the region on Thursday, ranging from a 0.36 percent drop in Hong Kong's Hang Seng index to a 3.8 percent plunge in the Kuala Lumpur Composite Index at the midday 0430 GMT break.
Against the bearish grain, South Korean shares soared 3.05 percent to 704.74 at 0522 GMT on hopes a rising yen could help boost earnings at domestic companies.

Elsewhere at midday, Singapore shares fell 1.44 percent, Japan's Nikkei 225 shed 1.63 percent, Taiwan sank 2.27 percent and Jakarta's stock index slipped 1.0 percent. Philippine shares closed down 2.77 percent on the Thai worries.
Domestic factors also played a part in market declines. Jakarta shares were hurt by rising political tensions, while profit-taking in the electronics sector hit Taiwan's market.
Alfred Lo, fund manager of ImPac Asset Management in Hong Kong, has $100 million invested in the region excluding Japan.
Picking markets within the battered Southeast Asian sector, he said: "We like Singapore by default. It's never been an exciting market but it's quite unlikely we are going to get nasty surprises."

The regional decline could be due to "one or two very big sell programs," said an equity strategist at a foreign brokerage firm in Kuala Lumpur. "I think people are getting jittery with the baht and Thailand and can't be bothered (with the region)."
But opinions were mixed as to whether Thursday's selling marked a pullout of the region.

Liew Yin Sze, chief economist at J.M. Sassoon in Singapore, believes there has been a sea change in views. "I think the weakness in the baht jolted a lot of institutional investors. They are saying if it can happen to Thailand, which country will be next?
"I think it's an rethinking of the entire reasons of why to invest in Asia," he said.
But Hugh Young, managing director at Abtrust Fund Managers in Singapore, which has about $850 million in Asia excluding Hong Kong, thinks otherwise.
"Yes, people are worried but I don't think there's a major shift going on at the moment. We are staying put. I think there are always people looking for reasons to shift."
